articles.title: People in Clacton react to Nigel Farage's by-election win
articles.summary: The Reform leader wins the by-election he triggered, and gains more votes than last time.
articles.body:
People in Clacton-on-Sea have woken up to the news that Nigel Farage will be returning to Westminster as their local MP.

The Reform UK leader secured 22,239 votes in the by-election he triggered by resigning in July, beating the 9,455 for second-placed Count Binface .

It was the culmination of a showdown in the Clacton constituency, which was boycotted by the other major British parties. Farage won more votes than he did when those parties stood against him at the 2024 general election, when he got 21,225 crosses on a much higher turnout of 58%, compared to 44% on Thursday.

However, a parliamentary investigation into Farage, who resigned the seat amid a row over his financial support, will now continue.

What do people in the Essex town make of the by-election result?

It was a "good result for Nigel", said Zak Apsey, but "it shouldn't really have needed to happen".

He argued the investigation into Farage was "not a big deal".

The Reform leader did not attend the result declaration, with his party saying the police had advised against it.

However, the BBC understands this was not the case.

"I wasn't disappointed he wasn't at the count. He was at his event, which is fine," Apsey added.

"He was still in the constituency, so what's the big deal?"

Jenny Hopkins, who made the trip to Clacton from Gloucestershire, said she was "delighted, absolutely thrilled" with the result.

"The fuss they've made about this so-called donation, gift or whatever it is - I think it is ridiculous," she said.

"This has proved the people of Clacton want Nigel Farage. However many by-elections they have, I think he'll win."

Linda Robinson felt the by-election was unnecessary and said she was not a fan of Farage.

"He's never here, is he? He's never in Clacton," she said.

She said that would be "all well and good" if her MP achieved great things for the town, but she said she did not believe he had.

Max Barrett was one of those people who voted for self-styled intergalactic space warrior Count Binface.

"It would be nice if he won, because it would be good for the area," Barrett said.

"There'd be a lot more tourism and it'd just be interesting him representing this area."

The Clacton resident said despite split opinions on the by-election, there were plenty of positives to take out of it.

"The whole community has come out. We're all talking to each other, which is very nice, no matter the difference in opinion," he said.

"We haven't had that for a very long time."

Some people in Clacton felt they were being used as part of a political "game", according to Sue Wackett, 70.

She felt let down by the Conservatives, Labour, the Liberal Democrats and Greens for not fielding candidates.

"It's got really nasty and for the first time in our lives, we try not to get involved in politics because it's scary," said Wackett.

"We need to all rethink and start thinking of each other as human beings, all entitled to our own opinions."

"I think the other parties were cowards not to stand," said Mary Williams, who travelled to Clacton from Wales to support Farage.

"They've tried to make it into a circus. They're all absolutely convinced he's going to be found guilty of something."

Pressure on Farage intensified after the Sunday Times reported he had not declared benefits , including staff and security, supplied with help from his long-term ally George Cottrell.

He has also faced questions about a Â£5m gift from cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne in early 2024, which he did not register.

"I'm worried. I'm really concerned because I think Nigel Farage is the only answer, the only hope we've got in Great Britain," Williams added.

BBC East's political editor Andrew Sinclair has given his thoughts on how local issues have taken a backseat during this by-election campaign, unlike many other recent by-elections in the region.

articles.title: The execution of Leslie James, the last woman hanged in Wales
articles.summary: Leslie James was executed for murder, but her looks were talked about as much as her crime.
articles.body:
As Leslie James was marched to the gallows on the morning of her 40th birthday, she could never have known her death would put her name in the history books.

On 14 August 1907 at 08:00, James was led from the women's block of Cardiff Prison to a shed which housed the gallows, suspended above a 15ft-deep (4.5m) pit.

There waiting for her were Henry and Tom Pierrepoint - a surname synonymous with the noose - and with that pull of the lever, James would become the last woman to be hanged in Wales.

In June of that year, she was accused of deliberately smothering a day-old baby girl as part of what the police and press called a "baby farming" conspiracy.

But a new book by author Mary Jones casts doubt on details surrounding the case, highlighting James's previously unreported brain injury, and how her looks were as much the focus of the press attention as her crime.

In The Execution of Leslie James, Jones documents how in the months leading up to her crime, Leslie James, or Rhoda Willis as was probably her real name, was hit by a bike, giving her such severe concussion that she was in hospital for three months.

She argues: "Whatever Leslie's culpability in her crimes, this surely ought to have been taken into account."

James stood trial at the July 1907 Swansea Assizes accused of murdering baby Treasure, who was only identified by the surname of her mother, Maud Treasure from Fleur-de-lis in Caerphilly.

The prosecution claimed James responded to a newspaper advert asking for someone to take care of an unwanted baby, offering £6 initially, and a further £2 at a later date.

At the time, "baby farming", where "inconvenient" children were offered up for money, was seen as a social scandal.

After collecting the child, it was alleged that James smothered her on the train journey back to Cardiff, most likely around Llanishen.

Most damningly for James, evidence emerged that she had previously taken on two other babies in similar circumstances.

After a trial lasting one-and-a-half days, the all-male jury took just 12 minutes to convict her, in what must have seemed like an open-and-shut case in those days.

In passing sentence, the judge said: "Don't let anyone suppose that because you are convicted of murder that nobody pities you, nobody prays for you.

"I implore you to employ the short time that is left to you to prepare for death and for that mercy which you will undoubtedly find in heaven, but which you cannot expect here."

Jones believes there were serious flaws in the trial, most importantly that James's brain injury was not mentioned as an explanation for her reckless behaviour.

"Her barrister, Ivor Bowen, was only appointed on the morning of the trial on the judge's orders and, as such, there was no time to speak to Leslie or call any defence witnesses.

"Had they have done so, then the jury would have heard what baby Treasure's family told the police, that the child was already frothing from the mouth, possibly because of the indigestible sugar-water mix which they had given her because her mother was unable or unwilling to breastfeed her, and also that she had been extremely tightly swaddled, so that neighbours could not tell that the package being handed over to Leslie was a baby.

"Either of these could have led to baby Treasure choking or suffocating, though Leslie didn't help her own defence insofar as she was an alcoholic and, I believe, honestly couldn't recall how the infant died on that journey home."

Jones added that, while James's two previous forays into baby farming were used in evidence against her, the counter argument was never put forward.

She left a note requesting medical assistance for the first child, who she left on the steps of the Salvation Army, and the second was thriving after being adopted by her landlady, Mrs Wilson at 132 Portmanmoor Road in Splott, Cardiff.

On the evening of 3 June 1907 James returned home but couldn't sleep in her own bed, and instead bunked up with fellow lodger Rose Smith.

The following day she went out and got "paralytically drunk".

As Mrs Wilson tried to help her into bed, she discovered a tightly-wrapped parcel, which at first she thought to be a cut of meat, only to discover the truth and informed the police.

"She is most likely to have been born in Sunderland in 1863, though she claimed to have been educated in a London boarding school," said Jones, who believes there may be evidence to support this.

"Rhoda/Leslie appears from the records to have been a highly literate and articulate lady and far removed from the common-or-garden 'hussy' or 'fallen woman' which the press chose to stereotype such so-called baby farmers."

Jones said when James was arrested she gave her name as Leslie James, but on previous public documents she was variously listed as Rhoda Willis/Dalzell/Lascelles, daughter to a jeweller, Ernest Dalzell, which may have provided her with a more affluent background.

While living a "blameless life" prior to the bike accident, by 1907 she had fallen into "troubled ways".

She was locked in a love triangle with Scottish-born brothers Stewart and McGregor McPherson, between whom she bore two babies.

Jones said that by the time she sought lodgings at Portmanmoor Road, she was already deeply damaged.

"The way she sought shelter in Rose Smith's neighbouring room shows that she knew something terrible had happened, but it also lends evidence to the conclusion that she hadn't intended for it to happen.

"Surely, if Rhoda had have been guilty of murder, then she wouldn't have drawn such attention to herself."

Cardiff council, her own solicitor Harry Lloyd, and the general public raised a petition of about 50,000 names to spare her life.

A 1,000-strong crowd outside the prison were mortified when a guard pinned the notice of her death to the gates.

Home Secretary Herbert Gladstone had, the night before, concluded that she be made an example of because of the "despicable practice of baby farming prevalent in south Wales".

Jones said: "I am seeking an apology for the fact that such a troubled woman was hanged without evidence that she'd ever committed murder.

"It is beyond doubt that baby Treasure died while in the care of Rhoda, but her degree of culpability is very debatable, at the very most she is guilty of manslaughter."

Jones said a degree of misogynistic fetishism saw James go to the gallows.

"All the press reports and even the hangman Henry Pierrepoint remarked on her beauty and composure.

"No male's demeanour had ever been commented upon so much in the papers: 'From the way in which the sunlight caught her auburn hair to her composure at the moment the lever was pulled.'

"She was made to stand out for some sort of message."

Now, 119 years after she died, the only physical record of James's grave is an etched cross next to a potato patch within the walls of Cardiff Prison.

articles.title: Corey Ruiz funeral to be held in Madison after fatal police shooting
articles.summary: A 38-year-old Black man who was shot and killed by police in Madison, Wisconsin, was laid to rest Friday.
articles.body: A 38-year-old Black man who was shot and killed by police in Madison, Wisconsin, was laid to rest Friday. Corey Ruiz, 38, was fatally shot after he pulled out a knife in a struggle with four police officers last month, according to authorities. Bystander video of the incident went viral on social media, prompting a series of protests in the Midwestern city and drawing fresh scrutiny over the harsh police tactics used on the city’s people of color. The video of his death raised questions about why lethal force was used after Tasers were deployed. The funeral was attended by civil rights lawyer Ben Crump, who is representing Ruiz’s family, and the Rev. Al Sharpton, who delivered the eulogy. Relatives of Ruiz’s also spoke. His mother, Elsa Ruiz, said her son was homeless and treated like “he was just a piece of trash,” Wisconsin Public Radio reported. “He was not a piece of trash,” she said, according to WPR. “He was not a nobody. He was my son.” Before the open-casket funeral began, Sharpton told reporters that he came to Wisconsin after watching bystander video of the shooting, WPR reported. “This could be my brother,” Sharpton said. “This could be my nephew, and the fact that my name is Sharpton and their name is Ruiz means nothing to a cop that will unload and shoot multiple times, when they could have talked to him, they could have done multiple things.” Madison police say that on July 22, officers approached Ruiz after receiving calls reporting that someone was stealing bicycles and checking vehicle doors. Authorities said that after initially fleeing, Ruiz pulled out a knife during a struggle with officers and injured one of them. Officers said they tried but failed to shock Ruiz with a Taser before shooting him. As of Friday, no arrests have been made in connection with Ruiz’s death. When asked about potential arrests, a spokesperson for the Madison Police Department said in an email that “the investigation remains with DCI at this time,” referring to the Wisconsin Justice Department’s Division of Criminal Investigation. “DCI will then turn things over to the District Attorney’s office who will make a charging decision,” the spokesperson, Officer Stephanie Fryer, said. The Division of Criminal Investigation did not immediately return a request for comment. Ruiz’s case was not the first high-profile killing of a Black man at the hands of a police officer in Madison. Tony Robinson was fatally shot by police in 2015, roughly a block and a half from where Ruiz was killed. And in 2012, Paul Heenan was killed by a police officer nearby. Wisconsin public records show that Ruiz was convicted of 40 misdemeanors and felonies from 2009 to 2025, including robbery by force and strangulation. Ruiz’s ex-girlfriend, who is the mother of his teenage daughter, previously told NBC News that Ruiz struggled with mental health issues, but declined to provide specifics. She said he was killed blocks away from where his daughter lives. “She has to walk past his dying grounds and that memorial every day when she starts school,” she said. “Every day, she has to walk past that to get to school.”

articles.title: Draft dark skies guidance drawn up for the Highlands
articles.summary: The plan to reduce light pollution could be put out for public consultation at a later date.
articles.body:
Highland Council has produced draft guidance aimed at reducing light pollution to give stargazers clearer views of the night sky.

Officials said other benefits of minimising outdoor lighting included lower carbon emissions and energy costs.

The guidance would support communities wishing to set up dark sky sites, which are locations with little or no light pollution.

Builders of major developments in, or near, dark sky sites would be required to carry out a lighting assessment to justify the need for exterior lights.

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

Councillors meeting next week have been asked to approve the draft guidance , external .

It would then be put out for public consultation before a finalised version of the document was produced.

The guidance could form part of Highland Council's proposed Highland Local Development Plan (HLDP), which is due to be published next year.

The HLDP would set out areas of the region to be zoned for housing or other developments.

In a report, officials said the proposed guidance would encourage best practice by minimising exterior lighting to only what was necessary for safety and security.

They said: "There are environmental benefits in terms of reduced emissions and lower adverse impacts on humans and wildlife, financial benefits in reduced energy usage and bills, and tourism economy benefits in terms of retaining and enhancing visitors' ability to enjoy the night sky."

In the report, planting trees and adding fencing have been suggested as ways of reducing the glare of outside lights.

Officials acknowledged that some communities would prefer to have exterior lighting for safety reasons.

The local authority has previously said the Highlands, which has large, sparsely populated areas, offered astronomy fans some of the darkest skies in Europe .

In 2024, the Isle of Rum, which is in the Highland Council area, was named Scotland's first International Dark Sky Sanctuary by the organisation DarkSky International.

articles.standfirst: Agência concluiu que não há elementos para considerar que ferramenta viole regras de concorrência, mas determinou que operadoras devem ser transparentes sobre critérios usados para bloquear chamadas.
articles.summary: Em disputa entre Vivo e TIM, agência concluiu que não há elementos para considerar que ferramenta viole regras de concorrência, mas determinou transparência.
articles.body:
O sistema da Vivo contra ligações indesejadas que foi alvo de reclamações da TIM foi autorizado pela Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações ( Anatel ), que avalia adotar bloqueios parecidos nas demais redes de telefonia. (veja mais ao final)

O chamado "Vivo Anti-spam" é tema de processos administrativos da Anatel desde o início de junho. A alegação de ao menos sete empresas, incluindo a TIM, é de que o serviço impede ligações legítimas e cria barreiras artificiais para concorrentes da Vivo.

Tem alguma sugestão de reportagem? Envie para o g1

Mas, na última quinta-feira (13), a Anatel concluiu que não há elementos suficientes para considerar o Vivo Anti-spam uma violação de regras do setor e determinou que a empresa pode continuar usando sua ferramenta.

A agência esclareceu que a medida não dá às operadoras liberdade irrestrita para bloquear chamadas . E disse que sistemas contra ligações indesejadas deve considerar fatores como proporcionalidade, transparência e igualdade no tratamento entre empresas.

Ligações automáticas indesejadas, chamadas de "robocalls" — Foto: Fantástico

Por que recebemos tantas ligações indesejadas? E como evitar esse tipo de chamada?

Um dos pontos questionados pela TIM foi a decisão da concorrente de ativar o anti-spam por padrão para todos os clientes – a ferramenta tinha sido lançada em novembro de 2024, mas só passou a ser ativada automaticamente em maio de 2026.

A Vivo disse que a taxa de cancelamento do serviço por usuários é de apenas 0,007%, o que reforçaria sua aceitação pelo público.

A Anatel concluiu que a ativação automática reduz a exposição de consumidores "hipervulneráveis" e com baixo letramento digital a golpes . Na avaliação da agência, eles teriam mais dificuldades para usar a ferramenta se tivessem que habilitá-la por conta própria.

Mas o órgão determinou que a página sobre o anti-spam no site da Vivo deve ter "informações claras, ostensivas e de fácil compreensão sobre seu funcionamento, incluindo os critérios e parâmetros utilizados para definir o tráfego sujeito à filtragem".

Além da TIM, outras empresas que questionaram o sistema relataram à Anatel casos de bloqueio de ligações consideradas legítimas, como aquelas feitas por serviços públicos de saúde, segurança e educação.

As operadoras também questionaram a falta de clareza sobre como o sistema define quais ligações seriam bloqueadas . Em alguns casos, os números foram liberados após contato com a Vivo.

A principal questão na disputa entre as empresas é o critério usado para bloquear as ligações, explicou Eduardo Tude, presidente da consultoria Teleco, ao g1 no início de agosto.

"O anti-spam do telefone funciona como o do e-mail: de vez em quando, caem coisas que não deveriam ter caído. Não existe um anti-spam perfeito que vai bloquear só o que deve", afirmou.

"A Vivo não pode bloquear as chamadas legítimas. A Anatel vai ter que estabelecer algum mecanismo para evitar que isso aconteça", continuou.

Anatel avalia ampliar bloqueios contra spam

Ainda em sua decisão, a Anatel recomendou que outros departamentos da agência avaliem a possível adoção de critérios de bloqueio de ligações indesejadas do Vivo Anti-spam pelas demais redes de telefonia.

Na avaliação da agência, o alto número de chamadas sem identificação e sem interação efetiva, como as ligações mudas, "configura prática abusiva, que deteriora a comunicação e promove crise de confiabilidade entre os usuários".

O objetivo com a recomendação é estimular a criação de padrões para barrar robôs no recebimento de chamadas, protegendo usuários que não saberiam configurar bloqueios manualmente.

Isso significa que o modelo da Vivo deixaria de ser uma iniciativa isolada para se tornar um padrão para todas as operadoras .

O órgão afirmou ainda que a padronização no setor ajudaria a garantir igualdade de condições entre as empresas, evitando que regras de filtragem fiquem restritas a apenas uma operadora.

Empresas afirmaram que sistema anti-spam da Vivo impediu ligações legítimas — Foto: Priscilla Du Preez/Unsplash

articles.title: Inteligência artificial compra e destrói livros para treinamento | G1
articles.standfirst: Livreiros relatam pedidos suspeitos em grandes quantidades. Acredita-se que as obras estejam sendo usadas ​​para treinar chats de IAs como o Claude.
articles.summary: Empresas de inteligência artificial compram grandes volumes de livros usados para treinar modelos como o Claude, gerando debates sobre direitos autorais e preservação.
articles.body:
As livrarias de livros usados, conhecidas como sebos, tornaram-se um novo reduto para buscar o 'alimento' da IA — Foto: Getty Images

Algo misterioso vem acontecendo no mundo dos livros usados. Nos últimos meses, livreiros independentes têm observado um padrão estranho de compras, que resulta no envio de grandes quantidades de seus romances para armazéns distantes.

Em uma semana típica, Stuart Manley, da livraria Barter Books, em Northumberland, um condado no norte da Inglaterra, costumava vender entre dois e três mil livros. Mas um único pedido feito recentemente, por uma empresa canadense, igualou o volume que ele esperaria movimentar em sete dias.

Ele afirma que "nunca viu nada parecido em 30 anos no ramo de livros usados".

Manley não é o único. Livreiros de todo o mundo têm relatado megapedidos igualmente incomuns. Eles não sabem ao certo qual é o destino final de seus livros.

Mas a suspeita é que eles não estejam sendo comprados por leitores ávidos no exterior, e sim por algo mais com um apetite voraz por novas informações: a inteligência artificial (IA) .

'Workslop': os trabalhos malfeitos por IA que geram retrabalho, roubam tempo e custam milhões às empresas

Claude, rival do ChatGPT, vai revelar quem criou texto com IA; veja como vai funcionar

OpenAI, do ChatGPT, diz que IA pode adicionar R$ 1 trilhão ao PIB do Brasil em três anos

A ideia de que o aumento nas vendas de livros usados ​​está sendo impulsionado pelo crescimento explosivo da IA ​​remonta a uma decisão judicial nos Estados Unidos .

Em 2025, um juiz decidiu que o uso de livros adquiridos dessa maneira para treinar softwares de IA não constituía violação da lei de direitos autorais americana. A decisão foi resultado de um processo movido contra a empresa de IA Anthropic por três autores.

Em sua sentença, o juiz William Alsup afirmou que o uso dos livros dos autores pela Anthropic era "extremamente transformador" e, portanto, permitido pela legislação americana.

Quando os documentos judiciais foram tornados públicos no mês passado, revelou-se também que livros estavam sendo destruídos durante o processo de treinamento do chatbot de IA da Anthropic, o Claude.

"O Claude é treinado com uma combinação de dados da web disponíveis publicamente, conjuntos de dados adquiridos comercialmente e dados que nós mesmos geramos", disse um porta-voz.

Eles ressaltaram que a obtenção de livros para treinamento é uma prática amplamente utilizada em toda a indústria de IA. "Nenhum de nossos programas de aquisição de dados compra e destrói livros raros ou de antiquário", acrescentaram.

Ainda assim, a ideia de que livros estão sendo transformados em polpa de papel causa inquietação.

David Tobin, que administra a livraria Walden Books, no norte de Londres, também tem registrado vendas incomuns. "De certa forma, é muito bom vender alguns desses títulos que não eram comercializados há muitos anos, mas seria triste se eles acabassem sendo destruídos", diz ele.

Por que empresas de IA estão destruindo milhares de livros antigos ao redor do mundo

As dicas de uma neurocientista para atualizar o cérebro na era da inteligência artificial

Documentos judiciais relacionados ao caso da Anthropic revelaram que o projeto de ingestão de livros antigos era referido em comunicações internas da empresa como "Projeto Panamá".

Os documentos indicavam que o objetivo da empresa era "digitalizar de forma destrutiva todos os livros do mundo".

A digitalização destrutiva é o processo de enviar livros para locais onde possam ser digitalizados em escala industrial.

Isso inclui remover a lombada do livro para que todas as páginas possam ser digitalizadas rapidamente — e os restos, reciclados.

"Há muito mistério em torno do Projeto Panamá", diz Manley, da livraria Barter Books. "O nome é novidade para mim, mas a realidade do projeto não é. Ele tem sido objeto de muita discussão nos fóruns de livreiros."

Ele não sabe que seus livros estão sendo comprados para esse ou para projetos semelhantes de outras empresas de IA. Mas diz que também é difícil rastrear as vendas, que parecem aleatórias e "sem qualquer lógica aparente".

Elas variaram de textos obscuros em latim a romances de faroeste.

Especialistas afirmam que a diversidade de temas também aponta para a IA, uma vez que textos incomuns e raros poderiam fornecer material novo para aprimorar o treinamento de grandes modelos de linguagem — a tecnologia que sustenta ferramentas de IA generativa, como os chatbots.

A professora Emily Hudson, especialista em propriedade intelectual da Universidade de Oxford, afirma que as leis de direitos autorais no Reino Unido diferem das dos EUA.

"O ponto de partida no Reino Unido é que todos esses atos de cópia — criar a biblioteca de treinamento e realizar o treinamento — exigem a permissão do titular dos direitos autorais", diz ela.

Para os livreiros, isso representa um dilema.

Eles se sentem desconfortáveis ​​com a ideia de livros serem destruídos — mesmo reconhecendo que nem todo título precisa ser preservado.

"Uma obra acadêmica recente, publicada em uma tiragem de apenas cem exemplares — dos quais 75 já estão em bibliotecas —, pode ser muito rara no mercado; mas talvez não seja uma perda tão grande se um exemplar for destruído", diz Derek Walker, proprietário da livraria McNaughtan's, em Edimburgo, na Escócia.

"Mas temos — e já vendemos — livros que são, por exemplo, o único exemplar conhecido de uma edição do século 18. Seria um problema muito mais grave se um livro desses fosse comprado para ser destruído, depois de ter sobrevivido por tanto tempo."

Manley afirma que a reciclagem de livros é uma boa solução para muitos títulos que o público não quer mais em suas estantes, especialmente quando isso impulsiona os negócios.

"Algumas pessoas podem ter preocupações éticas sobre o destino dos livros e se eles serão destruídos", diz ele. "Mas o mundo não precisa mais de cinco milhões de exemplares de O Código Da Vinci . Já tive livros anunciados na internet por 20 anos que não foram vendidos até hoje."

articles.title: 'O Assunto': veja como pais podem aumentar segurança digital de crianças e adolescentes em 7 dicas | G1
articles.standfirst: Especialista aconselha, principalmente, configurar o celular de acordo com a idade do usuário, utilizar controles parentais e acompanhar o uso de aplicativos.
articles.summary: Especialista aconselha, principalmente, configurar o celular de acordo com a idade do usuário, utilizar controles parentais e acompanhar o uso de aplicativos.
articles.body:
Pais e responsáveis podem adotar medidas para aumentar a segurança de crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital, como configurar o celular de acordo com a idade do usuário, utilizar controles parentais e acompanhar o uso de aplicativos . As recomendações foram apresentadas pela jornalista Renata Cafardo no episódio desta sexta-feira (14) do podcast "O Assunto".

Renata é autora do livro "O algoritmo das famílias" e pesquisa a relação entre crianças, adolescentes, famílias e plataformas digitais.

Segundo ela, a supervisão dos responsáveis deve fazer parte da rotina familiar e ser adaptada à idade da criança ou do adolescente. Entenda as dicas:

1. Celular configurado com a idade correta

Uma das primeiras medidas recomendadas pela jornalista é verificar como o aparelho está configurado. Segundo Renata, o dispositivo deve estar associado à idade real da criança ou do adolescente, e não à de um adulto.

Isso permite que os recursos de proteção disponíveis no sistema sejam aplicados de acordo com a faixa etária. A configuração, porém, não é suficiente. Renata recomenda também o uso de controles parentais.

Os responsáveis podem utilizar ferramentas específicas ou recursos de controle parental disponíveis nos próprios sistemas operacionais.

Esses mecanismos permitem acompanhar a atividade digital e, em alguns casos, receber alertas sobre determinados conteúdos pesquisados ou acessados. Renata cita o aplicativo Qustodio , que ela afirma utilizar e recomendar.

Segundo a jornalista, a ferramenta pode enviar notificações aos responsáveis quando identifica pesquisas relacionadas a temas como violência, pornografia e saúde mental . Também é possível acompanhar pesquisas e vídeos acessados no YouTube.

3. Pais devem conhecer a senha do celular

Outra recomendação apresentada no podcast é que os responsáveis saibam a senha do celular usado pela criança ou pelo adolescente.

Para Renata, não deve existir uma expectativa de privacidade absoluta quando se trata de menores de idade e de um ambiente que pode oferecer riscos.

A supervisão, porém, deve ser explicada à criança. "Não é controlar, mas é supervisionar essa experiência digital", afirmou.

Segundo ela, os filhos precisam saber que o celular poderá ser acompanhado e entender que a medida tem como objetivo protegê-los.

Renata também recomenda que os responsáveis acompanhem periodicamente aplicativos usados pelos filhos, como o WhatsApp.

Ela defende que esse acompanhamento seja incorporado à rotina familiar, em vez de ocorrer apenas quando os pais desconfiam de alguma situação. A supervisão deve mudar conforme a idade.

Segundo a jornalista, crianças e adolescentes mais velhos podem conquistar gradualmente mais autonomia, mas ainda precisam saber que os responsáveis acompanham sua experiência digital .

Renata também alerta para o risco de transformar o celular em uma espécie de "babá digital". Segundo ela, se a família optar por permitir que a criança tenha um celular ou acesso a redes sociais, é necessário manter a supervisão.

A tecnologia, na avaliação da jornalista, não deve ser tratada apenas como uma forma de entretenimento que mantém a criança ocupada quando os pais não podem estar presentes.

Além dos controles tecnológicos, Renata destaca a importância da conversa dentro de casa.

Os responsáveis devem explicar os riscos existentes na internet de maneira adequada à idade da criança ou do adolescente. Ela compara a orientação sobre segurança digital a outras conversas que fazem parte da educação dos filhos, como aquelas sobre alimentação, bebidas alcoólicas, sexo seguro e outros riscos.

Para Renata, a tecnologia não pode ser tratada apenas como diversão. Você vai conversar sobre navegar no ambiente digital de maneira segura", afirmou.

A recomendação é que essa conversa seja frequente e acompanhe o desenvolvimento da criança.

Renata ressalta que a responsabilidade pela segurança digital de crianças e adolescentes não deve ser colocada exclusivamente sobre os pais.

Segundo ela, trata-se de um desafio de toda a sociedade, que precisa lidar com uma geração que já cresce conectada.

Ao mesmo tempo, os responsáveis precisam reconhecer que saber usar tecnologia não significa necessariamente ter maturidade emocional ou ética para lidar com ela.

Por isso, a combinação entre configuração adequada, controles parentais, acompanhamento e diálogo é apontada como uma forma de tornar a experiência digital de crianças e adolescentes mais segura .

articles.title: Who voted for Count Binface in the Clacton by-election and why?
articles.summary: Cheaper Flakes and using Adele to fund the NHS - voters on why they support a man dressed as a bin.
articles.body:
Self-styled intergalactic space warrior Count Binface finished second in the Clacton by-election on Thursday with 9,455 votes.

A record 34 candidates stood in the contest, but Binface and Reform UK leader Nigel Farage were the only contenders to secure more than 500 votes.

The other major UK parties boycotted the election, which was triggered by Farage's resignation as an MP in July, having won the seat from the Conservatives in 2024.

Binface has stood in various high-profile elections around the country in recent years. Before Clacton, his best results were more than 24,000 votes in the last two London mayoral elections.

With more candidates on the ballot than ever before, why did 26.9% of voters choose a man wearing a bin on his head?

First-time voter Ben Peters, 18, from Holland-on-Sea, said the election had been a "joke" since the start.

He said: "It was a bit of a thrill, but at the same time it felt almost pointless because I knew that, no matter what I did, Farage was going to get back into the seat."

Stephen Bear jailed over sex offender breaches

Has the by-election changed things for Clacton?

Anti-asylum protester who shoved police is jailed

Binface's policies had included nationalising the singer Adele, moving a pub hand dryer in Uxbridge and enforcing a 99p price tag on ice creams with 99 flakes.

Peters said: "Even if it means voting for Count Binface and getting 99p ice creams for 99 flakes, that is one more step than Nigel Farage has ever done for Clacton."

Alex Greenwood, from Thorpe-le-Soken, acknowledged some policies were "a bit silly" but the 18-year-old student argued there was an underlying logic to them.

"Nationalising Adele... all of Adele's song proceeds go to a private company which goes to shareholders and her songs are pretty much cultural icons," he said.

"It's not actually that far-fetched... why not have all that money go to the government which could be used on the NHS and stuff?"

Greenwood suggested his vote was partially a protest against Farage, whom he believes called the by-election to avoid scrutiny from the Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards .

He added: "I do like Binface. I don't like Farage all that much."

Before Farage quit his Clacton seat in July, Parliament's standards watchdog had been investigating him for not declaring a Â£5m gift he received from billionaire Reform UK donor Christopher Harborne before he became an MP.

He said the by-election was a "people versus the establishment" showdown, saying the "people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions".

Kerry Mitchell, who lives in Wix, said she had voted for Count Binface because he would have made for a "more credible, honest, responsible, not to say committed, MP than Nigel Farage".

The 61-year-old, who voted Labour in 2024, said: "Nigel Farage poses a real threat to democracy in the UK and if Binface had won, it would have put an end to him.

"And it also added some much-needed humour and lightness into politics.

"The world is in a very dark place at the moment, and a bit of levity and humour is fantastic, especially when you contrast it with the rhetoric of outrage, division and anger that we hear from the far-right."

Tracey Donovan, 61, also voted Labour in the last general election and decided to back Binface on Thursday because it was "the only viable alternative to Farage".

"I detest Farage and everything he stands for. He has done absolutely nothing for our constituency," she told the BBC.

"I want an MP who represents our area with the constituents' interests being addressed.

"He claims the establishment is against him, but he is the establishment."

Donovan, who has lived in Clacton her entire life, added she was pleasantly surprised by how many people voted for Binface.

"He had almost a third of the votes cast as supposedly a joke candidate, and I'm very pleased that it is only really just over a quarter of the constituency [voting] population who actively backed Farage and Reform," she said.

"Count Binface could have rid this town of its Little Britain label if more of the 55% who didn't vote at all had got out there and voted against Farage."

Salon owner Verda Rigby, who lives in St Osyth, used to vote for the Conservatives before she "became a socialist" and started supporting Labour.

In this election, however, as voting for Labour was not an option, the 66-year-old instead opted for Binface.

"I could have stayed at home, but we fought for the right to vote and, look, it was partly for the joke that Farage is," she said.

"And I despise the right-wing parties Reform, Restore, and Reclaim - it's like a bad pop group of numpties."

People in Clacton react to Nigel Farage's re-election

Philip Bird, 66, has lived in Clacton for 30 years and said he, too, would have voted for Labour if the party had stood a candidate in the election.

"I think it was absolutely right not to stand anyone because none of the major parties should have condoned this election," he said.

"It was farcical, completely unnecessary, and designed to distract attention, and it wasn't going to change anything, so I was quite comfortable voting for a satirical candidate.

"Farage has greatly harmed the conversation in this country, he has been a dreadful MP, he has done nothing for Clacton, and in reality his politics are precisely what Clacton doesn't need."

In a statement after his win on Friday , the Reform leader said: "The verdict is now in, and it is a convincing, overwhelming win, with more votes than we got in the general election of 2024.

"Today, the voters in Clacton have stuck up two fingers to the entire political establishment."

articles.title: Solar eclipse in the South West: Pac-man to Shinto myths
articles.summary: Thousands turned out to watch the solar eclipse in the South West; here's what they made of it.
articles.body:
People across the South West gathered to watch a rare solar eclipse on Wednesday evening.

The event began at approx 19:00 BST with the Moon passing between the Earth and the Sun, creating a crescent shape in the sky.

In Sidmouth, families gathered to watch the event, with children describing it as a "once in a lifetime opportunity" and others comparing the shape of the Sun to a banana.

One young girl, Charlotte, said: "It's really exciting because the next time I'll see one, I'll be a lot older. It's like a once in a lifetime opportunity."

Charlie described the atmosphere as "magical", and said: "The kids haven't stopped screaming and been dancing around since we've been here."

Some people marked birthdays and anniversaries during the eclipse, giving the evening a romantic significance.

One young girl named Alice described the eclipse as brilliant, and said: "It kind of looks like Pac-man", whilst another felt that the sun disappearing was "kind of scary".

Commander Dave Lee, Royal Navy Parachute Display Team, spent the event parachuting into Pendennis Castle at the beginning of the eclipse.

Lee was one of five members of the Royal Navy and Royal Marines jumping out of the small aircraft at about 6,000ft (1829m), before deploying their colourful canopies.

Lee said: "It is really a once in a lifetime experience, you have a very real feeling of immediacy and freedom, and you get a great view."

David Heathfield spent the event telling stories about the "rare" mythology surrounding eclipses, in particular, the story of Amano-Iwato - the Japanese goddess of the sun - who hid in a cave depriving the world of light.

"I had to go all the way to Japanese Shinto mythology to find it", he said.

In Cornwall, people gathered at locations including Bude and a stone circle on the moors, with one person describing the experience as "very strange" and "surreal".

Another person said: "I think it's very, very spiritual."

In West Penwith, Mark said wildlife appeared to react to the changing light, with birds returning to their roosts as the eclipse took place.

"All the birds have gone to bed," he said, adding that a flock of seagulls and choughs had been feeding on flying ants shortly before they returned to the cliffs.

articles.title: ‘Revenge is inevitable’: Iran ramps up propaganda war with violent billboards
articles.summary: Anti-U.S. messaging has intensified since the death of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, with artificial intelligence playing a major role.
articles.body: The billboards are state-sponsored, plastered across Iran’s capital and far from subtle. One features an image of President Donald Trump lying in a casket; another shows the White House on fire; a third is a parody of the American flag with skulls in place of the stars and bombs dropping from the stripes. Alongside ads for a multitude of products such as cars and shampoo, the giant billboards have become familiar sights to the people of Tehran in recent years. But since the country’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in an airstrike on the first day of the war launched by the United States and Israel, the messaging has become bolder and the tone more violent during the almost six-month conflict. Pictures of them captured by Iranian photojournalists over the last six months show people going about their daily lives next to the huge billboards with the violent imagery and messaging. One shows a busy intersection last month near Tehran’s central Enghelab Square, where a huge billboard featuring benign images of Khamenei was replaced with one of Trump lying in a casket, his hands together over his belly. In mock handwritten text, it refers to the sailors killed by a torpedo attack on the Iranian warship Iris Dena by the USS Charlotte attack submarine, along with a death threat aimed at Trump. Less than two weeks later, it was replaced by an image featuring Trump being strangled by several pairs of hands. “Revenge is inevitable,” a message in English said on it. A total of 17 U.S. service members have died since the start of the war with Iran, according to the latest figures issued by U.S. Central Command on July 18. On April 20, Iran’s semiofficial Mehr News Agency quoted Abbas Masjedi, the head of Iran’s Forensic Medicine Organization, as saying that 3,375 people had been killed in the war. Anti-American rhetoric has long been a staple of Iran’s messaging since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, and for more than three decades, a hand-painted mural parodying the Stars and Stripes has watched over passing traffic in the capital, Tehran. In place of the stars, skulls and bombs can be seen dropping from the stripes, which are emblazoned with the message “Down With The U.S.A.” across the middle. While that one is clearly painted, the more modern images appear to have been generated with the help of artificial intelligence, including one depicting the White House on fire. Written in Persian, the words “blood for blood” sit above the flames. Iran has used AI to boost its online propaganda efforts throughout the war, and one company, Explosive Media, has published dozens of Lego-inspired videos varying from short snippets to three-minute music videos mocking Trump and his administration. The company, whose work some have dubbed “slopaganda,” has told NBC News that it does not work for the Iranian government and that the government does not have a say in the content of its videos. Trump himself has posted plenty of AI-generated images, including some featuring Iran’s ships and energy infrastructure being blown up and taken over by the U.S. military.
